entry.evidence: The volumetric contents of these basins and their temporal distribution are compiled.

sequences.source_document: Kale & Patil Pillai 2022, published PDF (body) and publisher XML text (abstract, captions)

steps.action: Compiled formation thicknesses, exposure areas and available geochronology for the seven Purana basins from the literature and the authors' own observations, drawn as dated lithologs; concluded that inter-basin correlation holds only at group level.
steps.quote: compiled in the Supplementary Data, File 1 based on published literature and our own observations

steps.action: Computed preserved volumes from maximum formation thicknesses and the widest known exposure area per basin, split into five lithological categories by assigned proportions (total about 0.77 million km3).
steps.quote: computed using these thicknesses and the widest known area of exposure within the host basin

steps.action: Assigned a depositional age range to each group's volume from the available geochronology.
steps.quote: assigned its age-range of deposition based on available geochronology

steps.action: Checked the assigned age ranges against published compilations, including the first author's own earlier compilation.
steps.quote: These age-ranges compare well with those compiled by Kale (2016), Chakraborty et al. (2020).

steps.action: Estimated the maximum duration of deposition from decompacted thicknesses and cited sedimentation rates per lithology, then spread each group's volume evenly about its median age (from Kale 2016) into age-bin probabilities.
steps.quote: accounted for by taking on board the maximum possible duration of deposition

steps.action: Varied the age-bin width (50 versus 25 m.y.) and found no significant change in the gross pattern; adopted 25 m.y. bins.
steps.quote: We tested the age-probability distribution using age-bins of 50 m.y. and 25 m.y. but did not observe significant variation in the gross patterns

steps.action: Read the temporal distribution of total volume and identified the peaks P1, M1, M2 and M3, with near steady-state Neoproterozoic accumulation.
steps.quote: displays a major primary peak (M2) in the Early MPtz (1450 ± 50 Ma)

steps.action: Proposed that the peaks reflect greater supply combined with faster subsidence; supply from large emergent cratons or from weathering of high-relief regions are offered as alternatives.
steps.quote: may be interpreted to represent a convergence of greater supply and faster subsidence to create the required accommodation space

steps.action: Examined the relative proportions of the lithotypes as ratios to siliciclastics and interpreted the phases of carbonate, argillite and magmatic dominance.
steps.quote: We examine the relative proportions of the five categories of lithotypes from the Purana basins in two modes

steps.action: Compared the normalised Purana proportions with Ronov's global chart after mapping categories between the two; the Purana record fluctuates where Ronov's varies smoothly.
steps.quote: A comparison of the probability distribution of the Purana sediments with the Ronov chart is made using normalised values

steps.action: Explained the mismatch by auxiliary differences: absence of pelagic sediments in the Purana record, and smoothing and sample bias in the global data.
steps.quote: The smooth temporal progressions in Ronov chart may be attributed evening out of the global scale data as well as some sample biases.

steps.action: Interpreted siliciclastic spikes as regressions and carbonate peaks as transgressions; linked P1 and M3 to supercontinent dispersal onset and M1 and M2 to detrital supply during drift.
steps.quote: Such periods of excessive supply of detritus that exceeds available accommodation space are recognised as regression.

steps.action: Derived a generalised craton-margin basin model giving the expected lithotype proportions at each stage of basin evolution, used as a yardstick.
steps.quote: will vary from group to group within a basin depending upon the prevailing stage of basin evolution as hypothetically shown in Fig. 5

steps.action: Reported category-wise results (magmatics, cherts, carbonates, argillites, siliciclastics) with tectonic and eustatic interpretations.
steps.quote: The probability distribution of the contents of the Purana basins brings out the following aspects of the temporal distribution of the five lithological categories

steps.action: Compared the distribution with published supercontinent assembly and dispersal timeframes and with Bradley's passive-margin abundance curve.
steps.quote: A comparison of this distribution pattern with the global perspective of supercontinental assembly

steps.action: Attributed part of the deviations from global patterns to uncertainties in the volume computations and to imprecise ages.
steps.quote: A small part of the deviations from global patterns may be attributed to the uncertainties associated with the volumetric computations and paucity of precise ages

steps.action: Kept a close match between lithotype variations and supercontinent cycles, with at least three continent-scale transgressions and complementary forced regressions.
steps.quote: display a close match between the variations in volumes of different types of lithotypes and global supercontinental assembly and breakup events

steps.action: Estimated the required provenance area (at least 1.8-2 million km2) from a 1:10 depositional-to-provenance area ratio taken from the Amazon and Mississippi basins.
steps.quote: These two modern continental basins indicate a ratio of 1:10 for the depositional area to provenance area.

steps.action: Compared the required provenance with the cratonic area available on a paleogeographic assembly with paleocurrents, basin by basin; found a large shortfall except for the Kaladgi and Bhima basins.
steps.quote: there is a big gap between available provenance area within the Indian subcontinent and that required to feed

steps.action: Stated rival sources: active mobile belts with higher relief (ratio 1:5) or unfolded belts, a buried northward Bundelkhand extension, drifted blocks (China, Madagascar, Australia-Antarctica), lost northern India, or km-scale uplift and unroofing.
steps.quote: An alternative option would be to attribute the supply of sediments to rapid tectonic uplift and unroofing of magnitudes of a few kilometres

steps.action: Disfavoured the uplift and unroofing rival because no such exhumation is documented and it conflicts with the extensional basin setting; judged larger cratonic provenance, including drifted blocks, more plausible.
steps.quote: Such exhumation histories of the cratonic blocks have not been documented from these mobile belts during the Meso- and Neoproterozoic times.

steps.action: Refined the event scheme to four transgressions and three forced regressions, possibly merging the 1.3 and 1.1 Ga transgressions, and tagged most of them as eustatic.
steps.quote: It is likely that the two Late Mesoproterozoic peaks (1.3 and 1.1 Ga) may represent a single transgression

steps.action: Concluded that the Purana volumes require external cratonic sources since drifted from India, and that existing paleomagnetic reconstructions need reassessment.
steps.quote: External sources from cratonic blocks that have subsequently drifted away from India are essential to justify these volumes.

end.claim: The sediment volumes preserved in the Purana basins cannot have come only from provenance inside the Indian subcontinent; external cratonic blocks that later drifted away are required.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the provenance-area estimate from the modern 1:10 depositional-to-provenance ratio, there is no gap between required and available source area, and so no claim of external sources.

gates.evidence: The data were compiled from the literature and from the authors' earlier field studies, not gathered to test a hypothesis (pp. 2, 13). The provenance claim faced a comparison of required versus available area that could have shown sufficiency, but the ratio and the areas are loose analogues with no uncertainty (p. 11). Nothing is stated as fixed before the data; the bin width was tested after the fact (p. 5).

novelty_claims.quote: we (arguably for the first time) document how the net content variation on a continental scale varies in comparison to global models

limits: The supplementary files (thicknesses, volumes, age-bin workings) were not supplied, so the computations cannot be checked. The XML text contains only the abstract and captions, so most locators are printed pages. The volumes use maximum thickness times widest exposure area and carry no stated uncertainty; this volume sub-claim (about 0.77 million km3) is an estimate without resolution. The match of lithotype variations to supercontinent cycles and the transgression-regression scheme are sub-claims at best_explanation, with no formal statistical test. Inconsistency: the abstract says the volumes are at least 2 magnitudes larger than Indian sources can supply (§0 ¶2), while the body says available provenance is at least a magnitude smaller (p. 12). The 1:10 ratio rests on two modern rivers, and its citation (Dowdeswell et al. 2010) concerns the Fennoscandian Ice Sheet; inference: a possible citation mismatch. The age-range check (p. 5) compares against Kale (2016), which is also the source of the median ages, so it is partly circular (inference). In-text references to Fig. 2b and 2c on pp. 8 and 10 apparently mean Fig. 3b and 3c (inference). The paper calls the ~1.8 Ga transgression Early Mesoproterozoic, against its own Paleoproterozoic scheme. The acknowledgements say editor and reviewer suggestions improved the manuscript, but no review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. The ordering of steps follows the text; the actual order of work is not shown.

disagreements.support: The compiled geochronology is too coarse to support correlation finer than group level.
disagreements.quote: Formation-level correlations, although attempted earlier by some authors are not tenable given the coarse resolution and granularity of chronological data.

disagreements.target: Deep-marine carbonate and chert interpretation (Mukhopadhyay et al., 1996; Chaudhuri et al., 1999, 2012; Mukhopadhyay and Chaudhuri, 2003)
disagreements.support: The cratonic substrate and modern and ancient analogues allow an outer shelf or ramp origin instead.
disagreements.quote: the diagnostic features reported for ‘deeper marine sedimentation’ are equally possible to explain as products of outer continental shelf or ramp environments

disagreements.support: The normalised Purana proportions fluctuate and the carbonates decline, whereas the global chart is smooth and shows increasing carbonates; the difference is attributed to setting and global smoothing.
disagreements.quote: appears to diverge from the relative consistency predicted by Ronov charts on a global scale

disagreements.support: The M1 and M2 sedimentation peaks fall when passive-margin abundance is low; the authors explain this by Indian rift-drift margins or by extensive contiguous platforms.
disagreements.quote: MPtz peaks (M1 and M2) are located during a time when the passive margin abundance (compiled by Bradley, 2008) appears to have significantly declined

disagreements.target: Existing paleomagnetic reconstructions of Proterozoic supercontinents (e.g., Pradhan et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2004)
disagreements.support: The provenance shortfall requires adjoining continental blocks, especially north of India, which these reconstructions do not show.
disagreements.quote: [...] of the Proterozoic supercontinental assemblies do not provide any clue of such blocks and therefore are open to reassessment.

alternatives_considered.chosen: Five-fold lithological classification, with evaporites and other special lithologies not treated separately
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Separate treatment of evaporites, black shales and suspected glaciogenic sediments
alternatives_considered.reason: On a gross scale they are not likely to constitute a large volume

alternatives_considered.chosen: Porcellanites and silicified tuffs excluded from the chert category
alternatives_considered.reason: Recognised as ignimbrites or silicified acidic tuffs in later work

alternatives_considered.chosen: Outer shelf or ramp origin for the suggested deep-marine carbonates
alternatives_considered.reason: Underlain by a cratonic substrate; the features are explainable by shelf or ramp analogues

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Supply from large emergent cratonic areas, or weathering of high-relief regions adjoining craton margins
Lower Mesoproterozoic carbonate share from detrital influx pushing the clastic-carbonate boundary seaward, or from eustatic regression
Fewer passive margins explained by rift-drift of Indian cratonic fragments, or by extensive contiguous shallow platforms
1:5 ratio compensating for high-relief active mobile belts; unfolding of the belts
alternatives_considered.reason: Modern Amazon and Mississippi analogues; higher relief of compressional belts

alternatives_considered.chosen: Larger cratonic provenance, including drifted blocks
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Rapid km-scale uplift and unroofing of the adjoining mobile belts
alternatives_considered.reason: Such exhumation is undocumented and would require revising the extensional basin configuration

alternatives_considered.chosen: Possibly a single Late Mesoproterozoic transgression
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Two separate transgressions at 1.3 and 1.1 Ga
